perfinr

perfinr holds the tested, documented versions of the R functions in Personal Finance: a field manual. The book builds each calculation from scratch so you can see how the formula works. This package is for readers who want those same functions without copying code out of a chapter. It also suits anyone who wants small, transparent personal finance calculations in base R. The full documentation lives on the pkgdown site.

Installation

perfinr isn’t on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("mjfrigaard/perfinr")

perfinr has no dependencies beyond base R.

Example

The book’s first job example takes home $3,200 a month and pays $960 in rent. The question is how much of that paycheck rent claims.

Think of take home pay as a single bar. Rent is one slice of it, and the rest of the bar is what’s left for everything else:

percent_of_income() divides the width of the slice by the width of the whole bar, then multiplies by 100:

library(perfinr)
rent_share <- percent_of_income(expense = 960, income = 3200)
rent_share
#> [1] 30

Rent takes 30% of take home pay.

One call, every category

Most functions are vectorized, so one call can compare several options. The code below passes every category from the book’s zero based budget to percent_of_income() at once:

budget <- data.frame(
  category = c("rent", "groceries", "transport", "investments", "savings", "fun money", "other"),
  amount = c(960, 350, 300, 320, 320, 450, 500)
)
budget$percent <- round(percent_of_income(expense = budget$amount, income = 3200), 1)
budget
#>      category amount percent
#> 1        rent    960    30.0
#> 2   groceries    350    10.9
#> 3   transport    300     9.4
#> 4 investments    320    10.0
#> 5     savings    320    10.0
#> 6   fun money    450    14.1
#> 7       other    500    15.6

Together the seven categories claim 100% of take home pay, so every dollar has a job.

Conventions

The functions keep the names, arguments, and defaults from the book, so code from a chapter runs unchanged after library(perfinr). A few rules hold across the whole package:

Rule Example
Rates and returns are decimals 0.07 is 7%
rule_of_72() is the exception and takes a percent rule_of_72(7)
Ratio functions return percents percent_of_income(960, 3200) returns 30, not 0.3
Most functions are vectorized future_value(10000, 0.07, c(10, 20)) returns two values
A few functions take single values only income_tax(), raise_kept(), payoff_vs_invest(), first_payment_split()
A 0% rate returns the no interest answer mortgage_payment(120000, 0, 30) is 120000 / 360
Bad inputs stop early with an error text, NA, or a zero where a divisor is needed
